definition: Malediction means a spoken curse that wishes harm on its target.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word malediction. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know malediction should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The soccer manager's touchline malediction — may every referee's phone die in a strange city — made even the fourth official laugh.
An insult is milder than a malediction — it wounds the present moment and is done; a malediction wishes lasting harm onto its target's future.
Damnation goes further than a malediction — a malediction wishes ruin on someone; damnation is that ruin pronounced final, with no appeal left.

A curse is the everyday word for ill fortune wished on someone — you can mutter one in a parking lot. A malediction is the same wish delivered with formality and style, the word of ballads and old courtrooms. Every malediction is a curse; only the ceremonious ones earn the longer name.

A hex is a curse worked as a spell — it wants ritual, a charm, candles, and the words are optional. A malediction is entirely spoken: harm wished out loud onto its target, no ritual required. Objects and ceremony make a hex; pronouncement alone makes a malediction.

At the end of a long interview about boat-building, the oldest netmaker on the island straightened, set down her awl, and performed the malediction her grandmother had taught her against gear thieves.
It ran four full sentences, wishing torn sails, empty holds, and forgotten graves on any hand that lifted another family's nets, and it had a meter you could tap your foot to.
She was not angry at anyone that afternoon, she explained; the words were an heirloom, kept polished in case they were ever needed.
You could grumble at a thief any day, she said, but this was said in full, standing up, the way her grandmother had insisted it be said.
